common_name: Siloam French Marble Daylily (Cream Daylily with Red Veining)

planting.note: Plant dormant-foliage divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained soil in full sun; this compact Siloam-series diploid bulks up quickly and benefits from division every three to four years.

directions: Pauline Henry of Siloam Springs, Arkansas introduced this diploid Siloam-series daylily, prized for ivory-cream petals laced with fine red veining that converges into a subtle red eye above a green throat. Scapes carry each ruffled bloom for a single day over a steady early-midseason run in June and July, with the low, grassy clump rarely exceeding 16 inches in bloom. Like other Siloam cultivars it performs best in full sun with consistent moisture and rewards division every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous.

common_name: Siloam Jim Cooper Daylily (Red Daylily with Darker Red Eye)

planting.note: Plant dormant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained soil in full sun; this compact Siloam-series cultivar forms a tidy clump that divides easily every few years.

directions: Registered by Pauline Henry in 1981, this diploid Siloam-series daylily bears red, single-form flowers accented by a darker red eye zone above a green throat, opening on compact 12- to 18-inch scapes during the early midseason. It earned the American Hemerocallis Society's Honorable Mention in 1985 and Award of Merit in 1989, recognition typical of the Siloam Springs, Arkansas breeding program. The clump stays tidy and dormant through winter, dividing easily every few years to maintain bloom count.

common_name: Siloam Olin Frazier Daylily (Hot Pink Double-Form Daylily)

planting.note: Plant dormant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this multi-award Siloam selection holds its full double form best with consistent moisture.

directions: Introduced by Pauline Henry in 1990, this Siloam-series selection produces hot rose-pink double blooms roughly 5 inches across on scapes about 22 inches tall, flowering early in the season. The cultivar collected a Junior Citation in 1990, Honorable Mention in 1994, and Award of Merit in 1997 from the American Hemerocallis Society. Give it full sun to light afternoon shade and divide the dormant clump every few years to sustain its characteristically full, ruffled double form.

common_name: Siloam Show Girl Daylily (Ruffled Red Daylily with Dark Red Halo)

planting.note: Plant dormant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained soil in full sun; tolerant of clay and acidic soils once established.

directions: Hybridized by Pauline Henry and registered in 1981, this compact Siloam-series daylily opens ruffled red petals with a deeper red halo above a green-gold throat on scapes 12 to 18 inches tall. It blooms heavily through midseason, with each flower lasting only a day before the next wave opens, and tolerates clay and acidic soils once established. Full sun and routine division every few years keep the dormant clump blooming at its best, and the nectar-rich flowers reliably draw hummingbirds and butterflies.

planting.note: Plant dormant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained soil in full sun; this compact, long-blooming diploid is an easy front-of-border candidate.

directions: Hybridized by Clarence Reckamp and registered in 1963, this small-flowered diploid daylily blends melon-pink, cream, yellow, and orchid tones into a soft polychrome bloom centered on an orange throat. It won the American Hemerocallis Society's Annie T. Giles Award in 1967, an annual honor for the best small-flowered seedling. Compact scapes rise just over a foot above the grassy clump, making it a long-blooming front-of-border choice that divides easily in spring or fall.

planting.note: Plant dormant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; its diminutive, grass-like clump suits rock gardens and border edges.

directions: Bred by Ben R. Hager and registered in 1987, 'Penny's Worth' is a dormant diploid miniature daylily with grass-like foliage that stays under a foot tall even in bloom. Its circular, golden-yellow flowers, barely an inch and a half across with a deeper yellow throat, open in flushes from extra-early spring into summer, and the plant reblooms readily where moisture is adequate. Its diminutive scale makes it a natural choice for rock gardens and border edges.

common_name: Red Ribbons Daylily (Bright Red Spider-Form Daylily)

planting.note: Plant dormant divisions in spring or early fall in moderate, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; this tall spider-form cultivar benefits from staking in windy sites.

directions: Registered in 1964 by G.A. Lenington from a cross of 'Wanda' and 'Mabel Fuller', this tall spider-form daylily opens bright red flowers up to 8 inches across with long, narrow, gracefully twisting petals and a greenish-yellow throat atop scapes nearly 3.5 feet tall. Multiple buds per stalk and several stalks per clump extend the bloom season for two weeks or more from early to midsummer. It carries the American Hemerocallis Society's Harris Olson Spider Award along with Honorable Mention and Award of Merit honors, and performs reliably in full sun to light shade.

common_name: Hendersonii Rubra Armand Clematis (Pink-Budded Evergreen Spring Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade with a sturdy trellis, arbor, or fence; prune only right after flowering since buds form on the prior season's wood.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade against a sturdy trellis, arbor, or fence, since this vigorous evergreen Armand clematis selection can climb 15 feet or more. Hendersonii Rubra opens from darker pink buds into soft pink, star-shaped flowers carried in dense clusters on red-tinted stalks, with a sweet almond-and-orange-blossom fragrance that carries well through early spring. The leathery, trifoliate evergreen foliage takes on purple tints as new growth emerges, giving year-round structure even when the vine is not in bloom. Because flower buds form on the previous year's wood, prune only right after flowering to keep the vine in bounds.

common_name: Heather Herschell Clematis (Pink Bell-Flowered Viticella-Integrifolia Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with roots shaded and cool; cut the whole plant back hard in late winter since it flowers on new growth produced the same season.

directions: Bred by Barry Fretwell and introduced around 1999, this hybrid between Clematis viticella and C. integrifolia produces nodding, bell-shaped pink flowers with four ribbed, slightly notched sepals that recurve with age into a pagoda-like shape. Sweetly scented blooms appear from midsummer into early fall on lax, non-clinging stems that are best woven through herbaceous perennials or small shrubs for support. Cut the whole plant back hard in late winter, since it flowers on new growth produced the same season. It is a reliably easy, free-flowering choice for a mixed border where a true climbing clematis would be too vigorous.

common_name: Mongolian Bells Clematis (Compact Nodding Bell-Flowered Herbaceous Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this non-twining, compact integrifolia selection needs no climbing support and makes a good border filler or small-scale groundcover.

directions: Collected as seed in Inner Mongolia in the 1990s by Harlan Hamernik of Bluebird Nursery, this compact, non-twining form of Clematis integrifolia produces a profusion of nodding, bell-shaped flowers in shades of blue, lavender, purple, or white from late spring through summer. Staying only about a foot tall and wide, it needs no climbing support and works well as a drought-tolerant border filler or scrambling groundcover once established. Spent flowers give way to feathery, sphere-shaped seed heads that add interest into fall. It thrives with regular to low water in full sun to light shade and tolerates a wide hardiness range.

common_name: Warwickshire Rose Clematis (Pink Spring-Flowering Montana Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil with roots shaded; a pruning-group-one cultivar that needs no regular pruning beyond tidying after the spring bloom.

directions: Discovered and named by garden designer John Williams after his home county, this vigorous montana-type clematis was released in 1994 and quickly became one of the most popular spring-flowering climbers. Soft pink, star-shaped flowers with deeper pink centers smother the vine in a single dramatic flush during late spring, carrying a scent reminiscent of chocolate and vanilla, while new growth emerges tinged bronze-red. It climbs rapidly to 15 feet or more and belongs to pruning group one, meaning it needs no regular pruning beyond removing dead or overcrowded growth right after flowering. Give the roots a cool, shaded position while letting the top growth reach for full sun, and provide sturdy support for its twining leaf-stalks.
